I will keep my farm centered on the wheat-maize system, because in Quzhou County that is still the most reliable way for me to use the full year, match the local climate, and protect cash flow. At the start of the season I already have winter wheat in the field, so my first job is to push that crop to a stable yield with a moderate fertilizer program, a few irrigations timed around jointing and grain filling, and only targeted pesticide sprays when pressure justifies it. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize on the same land, because that rotation fits my machinery, labor schedule, and local market conditions. For maize, I will rely on hybrid seed, keep planting density and fertilizer balanced, and use no-tillage after wheat where I can to save time and conserve moisture.

I will also set aside a smaller block for spring peanut. I want that partly to spread risk and partly because it breaks the continuous cereal pattern, which helps with soil condition and disease pressure. I would not overpush inputs there; I would keep nitrogen low, emphasize phosphorus and potassium, and manage weeds and insects carefully. Overall, I am choosing a practical plan: most of my land stays in the proven wheat-summer maize rotation, and a smaller share goes into peanut for diversification and soil balance.
